title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Strictly Prohibiting Arbitrary Suspension of Payment under Letters of Credit
full_text_en:
Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Strictly Prohibiting Arbitrary Suspension of Payment under Letters of Credit

Fa [2003] No. 103

To all High People's Courts of provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; all Intermediate People's Courts and maritime courts that accept foreign-related commercial cases:

Since the beginning of this year, international steel market prices have dropped sharply. Affected by this, the prices of some domestic steel products in China have also shown a declining trend. The sharp narrowing of the gap between import costs and domestic sales prices has directly affected the commercial interests of steel importers. Some importers have therefore requested banks to find reasons in the documents to refuse payment abroad, or have sought some very far-fetched so-called "fraud" reasons to apply to courts for suspension of payment under letters of credit. Some courts have arbitrarily rendered rulings to suspend payment of the funds involved under the letters of credit, which has already caused adverse effects abroad. In order to safeguard the international image of our courts and our banks, we hereby notify as follows:

1. Strictly adhere to the principle of independence of letters of credit. A letter of credit is a documentary transaction independent of the underlying transaction. As long as the documents submitted by the beneficiary appear on their face to comply with the requirements of the letter of credit, the issuing bank is obliged to pay within the prescribed time limit. The letter of credit transaction and the underlying transaction belong to two different legal relationships. Under normal circumstances, a court shall not rule to suspend payment of funds under a letter of credit issued by the issuing bank merely because a dispute arises in the underlying transaction.

2. Strictly adhere to the conditions for the application of the fraud exception principle to letters of credit. Only when there is sufficient evidence proving the existence of fraud under the letter of credit, and the bank has not yet made payment abroad within a reasonable time, may the people's court, upon the request of the applicant for the letter of credit and on condition that the applicant provides security, rule to suspend payment of funds under the letter of credit. However, if the letter of credit has been accepted and transferred, or if the letter of credit has been negotiated, the suspension of payment shall still not be ruled.

People's courts at all levels shall attach great importance to the suspension of payment under letters of credit, and shall strictly prohibit arbitrarily ruling to suspend payment of funds under relevant letters of credit when conditions are not met. If an erroneous ruling of suspension of payment has already been made, the relevant people's court shall immediately correct it.

This notice is hereby given.

July 16, 2003
